name: Koti
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 1997. De Swahili-talen van Mozambique. Mededelingen van de Afdeling Letterkunde, Nieuwe Reeks 60(2). Amsterdam: Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen. 27 pp. (Dutch; open access, Leiden repository hdl:1887/8836; based on the author's 1993 and 1995 fieldwork in Angoche).
catalog_locator: p. 77, section on Koti-Makhuwa correspondences, paragraph immediately before 'Tabel 14. Focus-toonverlaging in Koti en Makhuwa' and the two paragraphs after the table.
catalog_quote: Een andere zeer specifieke overeenkomst Koti-Makhuwa ligt op tonaal gebied. Ik heb in mijn betoog tot nu toe toon buiten beschouwing gelaten: het Swahili is geen toontaal, maar het Makhuwa en het Koti zijn dit net als de meeste andere Bantu-talen wel. Het toonsystemen van het Koti is bijzonder nauw aan dat van het Makhuwa verwant. Ik geef slechts één enkel voorbeeld dat de gebieden fonologie, vervoeging en syntaxis raakt. ... In een aantal tenses maakt het Koti een tonaal verschil al naar gelang er wel of niet een focus op het object valt. ... Het woord voor 'kleren' is in het Makhuwa iküwo, met een hoge toon op de tweede klinker (mora), en het Koti-woord puüzi 'geit' heeft dezelfde tonale structuur. In beide gevallen doet "focus-lowering" deze hoge toon verdwijnen. [Translation: Another very specific Koti-Makhuwa correspondence lies in the tonal domain. So far I have left tone out of consideration: Swahili is not a tone language, but Makhuwa and Koti are, like most other Bantu languages. The tone system of Koti is particularly closely related to that of Makhuwa. I give just one example touching phonology, conjugation and syntax. ... In a number of tenses Koti makes a tonal difference according to whether or not there is focus on the object. ... The word for 'clothes' is in Makhuwa iküwo, with a high tone on the second vowel (mora), and the Koti word puüzi 'goat' has the same tonal structure. In both cases 'focus-lowering' makes this high tone disappear.]
world_status: statement found in an open source

Verbatim match with the text (the compiler bracketed '[sic.. = toonsysteem]' is an editorial note, not part of the quote). Read the surrounding section (pp. 76-78): it continues with the f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koti is described first-hand as a tone language of the Makhuwa type (two-level H/L system; per the summaries of Schadeberg & Mucanheia 2000: no lexical tone on verbs, morphologically assigned H, High Tone Doubling, utterance-final lowering), explicitly contrasted with non-tonal (penultimate-stress) Swahili; no source seen states a word-stress rule. The only remark on 'acento tonico' found is pedagogical: Abdul & Lyndon 2001/2010 p. 4 say that a word-final i does not attract the stress as it would in Portuguese (javali vs. Ekoti khaazi), which presupposes non-final (presumably penultimate/long-vowel) prominence in citation forms but gives no general rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Supplementary quote (SIL learner's manual, file, p. 4): 'Em Ekoti a letra i na posicao final nao muda o acento tonico na palavra como em Portugues. Ex. Portugues: javali - Ekoti: khaazi' and 'O Portugues emprega acentos.. para mudar o acento tonico na palavra.. Em Ekoti nao e preciso escrever estes acentos.'
new_statements.domain_note: Schadeberg's statement is a typological classification (word-level tone vs. Swahili stress), made in an academy lecture based on his own fieldwork; the full analysis is in Schadeberg & Mucanheia 2000 (chapter on phonology, tone and orthography) and Schadeberg 2000 'The tonal system of EKoti nouns', neither of which could be opened. Final Lowering in Ekoti is reported (second-hand, Patin 2016: 29; Wikipedia after S&M 2000) to target the utterance-final syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ekoti of Koti Island / Angoche town (koti1238; S&M 2000 data mainly from co-author Mucanheia, of Mulai, Angoche district, and Koti-island idiolects). The related coastal variety Enatthembo/Sangaji (Sakati, glottocode nath1238, ISO nte) is treated separately by Schadeberg and SIL and is not covered by the quoted statement.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2003. Makhuwa (P30). In Derek Nurse & Gerard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 546-565. London: Routledge.
sources.note: pp. 546-7: Koti 'clearly represents a mixed language in that it has a largely Makhuwa morphology and tone structure and a Swahili-like lexicon' (Kisseberth did his own Koti research with Mucanheia). The chapter's Makhuwa tone section (3.4: no lexical tone on verbs, predictable H assignment, High Tone Doubling) never mentions stress; Koti itself is not further described.

sources.note: p. 4 ('Pequeno Guia para Ler e Escrever a Lingua Ekoti'): 'Em Ekoti a letra i na posicao final nao muda o acento tonico na palavra como em Portugues. Ex. Portugues: javali - Ekoti: khaazi'; 'Em Ekoti nao e preciso escrever estes acentos.' I.e. i-final words are not final-stressed as a Portuguese reader would expect (implies non-final, presumably penultimate, prominence); no general stress rule given. Tone remarks: 'Os tons dos numerais 1,2 e 3 sao baixos'; 'a tonalidade dos locativos e complexa'.
